The digits as written give 36 bits, so 'as written' is loosely worded. S2 src/lib/sv-timescale-model.ts:453-460 (asserted by tests/lib/sv-timescale-model.test.ts:1121-1135) - for an unsized signed literal from 2^31 to 2^32-1, the new branch tells the learner the sign depends on the width the tool picks, and that 'at exactly 32 bits it is -1'. The code comment adds that 'a 32-bit tool conforms'. This leaves out the next sentence of IEEE 1800-2023 §5.7.1, which reads: 'An unsized number that requires more than 32 bits shall have at least the minimum width needed to properly represent the value, including a sign bit if the number is signed'. The clause's own example says 4294967296 (2^32), a positive signed integer, 'shall be represented by at least 34 bits', so the sign bit counts toward the width. A signed 4294967295 therefore needs 33 bits, and a 32-bit width does not conform. For #('sd4294967295) the lab's '-1 at exactly 32 bits' teaches a reading the clause rules out. For 'sh/'sb/'so the same sentence points to the positive reading, and the lab does not cite it. -> Fix: send the 'sd (decimal-base) case to the positive branch ('Its value is 4294967295, so write #4294967295 instead'). For the b/o/h case, quote the §5.7.1 sign-bit sentence and its 2^32 -> 34-bit example, say which reading it supports, and note the open question (the s designator 'does not affect the bit pattern specified, only its interpretation') as uncertainty, not as a conforming 32-bit option. Remove the 'a 32-bit tool conforms' comment. Update the ['#(\'sd4294967295)', ..., '-1'] row of the test to match.

Verified correct against the sources (no action): 1800-2023 §5.7.1. The size is a nonzero unsigned decimal, and A.8.7 has 'size ::= unsigned_number', so 04'bx and 0_8'hz are legal and 0'bx and 00'bx are not. White space is allowed between the size and the apostrophe and before the value (example '5 'D 3'), but not between the apostrophe and the base letter. A.8.7 footnote 53 bars white space after the apostrophe of an unbased unsized literal. Left padding is with 0, or with x/z when the leftmost bit is x/z, and a value longer than the size is truncated from the left. The s designator changes only the interpretation (two's complement; example '4 'shf' = -1). Unsized numbers have at least 32 bits, and a wider value is never truncated. Other checks: A.2.2.3 delay_value is unsigned_number | real_number | ps_identifier | time_literal | 1step. 1step occurs nowhere else in the grammar and is absent from A.8.4 primary_literal (number | time_literal | unbased_unsized_literal | string_literal), so #(1step) is illegal. unbased_unsized_literal ('0 | '1 | 'z_or_x) is separate from integral_number. §5.8 interprets a time literal as a realtime value scaled to the current time unit. §6.11 Table 6-8 makes time a 4-state 64-bit unsigned integer. §20.3.1 says $time returns a 64-bit time scaled to the time unit of the invoking module. §9.4.1 sizes a negative delay like a time variable and interprets an x/z delay as zero. Under §11.8.1, if any operand is real, the result is real, which justifies 5000.0/1000.0. The §22.7 example (`timescale 10 ns / 1 ns, parameter d = 1.55, #d twice, 16 ns) matches the reworded running-total feedback. The same-slot distractor is offered only when 0 is not a candidate, so 'more than half a tick' holds. The running-total option is dropped only when a total is a tie that the half-to-even and away-from-zero rules round apart (#0.125 at 10ns/1ns, 2.5 ticks).

I checked both findings against t1_lrm_clean.txt, §5.7.1. Both are correct, and I fixed both at the cause.

The source says that an unsized number needing more than 32 bits gets the minimum width that represents its value, 'including a sign bit if the number is signed'. Its example, 4294967296 (2^32) as a positive signed integer, takes at least 34 bits. The same clause says 'The s designator does not affect the bit pattern specified, only its interpretation'.
